source.title: Scaling-up Diverse Orthogonal Convolutional Networks with a Paraunitary Framework
source.authors: Jia-Hao Su; Wonmin Byeon; Furong Huang

record.tranche_reason: The paper trains orthogonal convolutional networks on CIFAR-10 and reports training accuracy across margin settings, a different training recipe from the versions’ general claims.
record.gate_note: Training accuracy is shown only in Figure 7; text says it rises with larger margin. Test accuracy comparisons for skip connections, depth, width, and initialization do not measure training error and are not rows. Orthogonality and robustness results do not measure the claimed behavior.
record.test_reason: Figure 7 measures CIFAR-10 training classification accuracy after Adam training in a new setting: orthogonality-constrained Lipschitz WideResNet22-10 networks with multi-class hinge loss. This bears on V1, but the supplied text does not establish whether training error approaches zero.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but abbreviated. The authors establish a paraunitary framework for orthogonal convolution variants and use it to scale orthogonal networks while preserving Lipschitz bounds. Their complete multidimensional construction covers separable systems. Figure 7 separately states that training accuracy increases with larger hinge-loss margins.
record.recipe_differences: Orthogonal convolutional networks trained on CIFAR-10 with Adam and multi-class hinge loss; training accuracy is shown across margin settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported training accuracy changes with the multi-class hinge-loss margin.

fits_no_version.finding: Additive skip connections improve clean and robust test accuracy over concatenative connections and no shortcuts (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additive skip connections improve predictive performance in the tested deep Lipschitz networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Depth, width, and initialization comparisons report clean and robust test accuracy (Tables 5–6), without training-speed or training-error comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture and initialization choices affect predictive performance in orthogonal Lipschitz networks.

fits_no_version.finding: SC-Fac achieves machine-precision layer orthogonality and improves computational scalability relative to previous orthogonal convolution designs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Paraunitary parameterization enables precise and efficient orthogonal convolution layers.

record.problems: The only directly relevant training-accuracy result is figure-only and has no stated numeric values; the paper’s other accuracy comparisons report test accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No rows extracted: Figure 7 shows training accuracy by margin, but does not give numeric values and the text does not state whether training error approaches zero. Other reported comparisons use test accuracy, which does not measure the claim’s training-error outcome.

untested.parts: CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, smaller-model and early-stopping comparisons, and unconstrained convolutional training recipes. Near-zero training error cannot be determined from the supplied rendering of Figure 7.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious local minima, and extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth and its prevention by identity shortcuts; the architecture comparisons report test accuracy.
Initialization effects on training speed or trainable depth, activation-matched initialization, and orthogonal versus matched-variance Gaussian initialization.
Stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature trajectories, and divergence.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparisons with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is justified: the Figure 7 caption gives a direction of change, but neither readable training-accuracy values nor an explicit near-zero-error conclusion. The figure's omitted results are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not added to missing. Test accuracy cannot establish V3 or V4. Section 6.3 names identical initialization as best, whereas Appendix D.2 names permutation; Table 6 reports different winners for clean and robust accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports training accuracy only as a figure without numeric values or a textual statement establishing whether training error is near zero. It does not test CIFAR-100, corrupted or random labels, smaller models, early stopping, or the SGD recipes named in the version.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width are not tested.
The paper compares skip-connection types and network depths using predictive accuracy, not training error; it does not test the stated plain batch-normalized versus residual comparison.
Initialization methods are compared on predictive accuracy, not training speed or trainable depth; the stated plain tanh and 10,000-layer convolution experiments are not tested.
Learning rates above a stability threshold, curvature changes, and edge-of-stability behavior are not tested.
Batch normalization speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup without normalization, are not tested.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
